decks.module: More ways to lose your license
decks.domain: License loss, seat belts and impaired driving

cards.front: Can unpaid court-ordered child support affect your Colorado driving privilege?
cards.back: Failing to pay court-ordered child support is another way to lose your Colorado driving privilege.

cards.front: What must you carry while driving, and what happens if you cannot show it to an officer?
cards.back: You must carry proof of insurance whenever you drive, and failing to show valid evidence of insurance when an officer asks can cost you your license.

cards.front: Can an under-age alcohol purchase or possession conviction cost your driving privilege?
cards.back: A conviction for buying or possessing alcohol while under twenty-one can also lead to losing your driving privilege.

decks.domain: License loss, seat belts and impaired driving

cards.front: Who must wear a fastened seat belt on Colorado public roads?
cards.back: On public roads, Colorado requires a fastened seat belt in every vehicle with factory-installed belts for the driver, every front-seat passenger, and every child under sixteen.

cards.front: Who is exempt from Colorado's seat belt rule?
cards.back: The only seat belt exceptions are emergency personnel, passenger and school buses, farm equipment, delivery-van drivers while working, and anyone carrying a physician statement saying they cannot wear a belt for physical or psychological reasons.

cards.front: When is a delivery-van driver exempt from wearing a seat belt?
cards.back: Seat belts are required for the driver, front-seat passengers and children under sixteen, but delivery-van drivers are exempt only while on the job.

cards.front: When the driver is under eighteen, who must be belted and how many passengers may ride?
cards.back: When the driver is under eighteen, every passenger must be belted or properly restrained, and the passenger count may never be more than the number of seat belts.

decks.module: Child restraints by age and weight
decks.domain: License loss, seat belts and impaired driving

cards.front: Who must make sure children are properly restrained when no parent is in the vehicle?
cards.back: When no parent is in the vehicle, the driver is responsible for making sure each child is properly secured in the correct child restraint.

cards.front: How must a child under two who weighs under forty pounds ride?
cards.back: A child younger than two who weighs less than forty pounds must ride in a rear-facing child restraint in the back seat.

cards.front: What seat may a child under two who weighs forty pounds or more use?
cards.back: A child younger than two who weighs forty pounds or more may ride in either a rear-facing or a forward-facing child restraint.

cards.front: For a child under two, what decides rear-facing only versus either direction?
cards.back: The rear-facing rule for a child under two turns on weight: under forty pounds means rear-facing in the back seat, while forty pounds or more allows rear-facing or forward-facing.

cards.front: What restraint does a child aged two to under four, at least twenty pounds, need?
cards.back: A child aged two to under four who weighs at least twenty pounds must ride in a rear-facing or forward-facing child restraint, in the back seat when one is available.

cards.front: What does a child aged four to under nine, at least forty pounds, need?
cards.back: A child aged four to under nine who weighs at least forty pounds must use a child restraint or booster seat in the back seat when the vehicle has one.

cards.front: Which age band has the twenty-pound minimum and which has the forty-pound minimum?
cards.back: The twenty-pound minimum belongs to the age two to under four band, while the forty-pound minimum belongs to the age four to under nine band that allows a booster seat.

cards.front: How must children from nine to eighteen be restrained?
cards.back: Children from nine to eighteen must be restrained by a seat belt or a child restraint used as the manufacturer directs.

decks.domain: License loss, seat belts and impaired driving

cards.front: Why is impaired driving such a serious safety problem?
cards.back: Impaired driving by alcohol, drugs or a mix of them is among the leading causes of crashes and deaths on the road.

cards.front: What kind of drug is alcohol, and what does it do to a driver?
cards.back: Alcohol is a depressant: it slows brain function, reflexes and reaction time, harms thinking and coordination, and makes risky moves such as speeding or abrupt turns more likely.

cards.front: Where in a vehicle is an open container of alcohol or marijuana illegal?
cards.back: It is illegal to have an open container of alcohol or of marijuana in the passenger area of a vehicle on a public road.

cards.front: What determines a person's blood alcohol concentration?
cards.back: BAC depends on how much you drank, your body weight, how fast you drank, how long since the last drink, and your sex, so two people drinking the same amount can differ.

cards.front: Is beer less intoxicating than wine or liquor per standard drink?
cards.back: Beer, wine and liquor are equally intoxicating per standard drink: twelve ounces of beer, five ounces of wine and one point five ounces of distilled spirits each hold about the same alcohol.

cards.front: Does switching from liquor to beer make drinking and driving safer?
cards.back: A standard drink is the same alcohol whether it is twelve ounces of beer, five ounces of wine or one point five ounces of spirits, so switching drink types does not make you safer.

cards.front: What is the only thing that lowers your blood alcohol concentration?
cards.back: Only time sobers you up, and on average BAC falls by about zero point zero one five percent per hour.

cards.front: Can coffee or a cold shower speed up sobering?
cards.back: BAC drops only with time, at about zero point zero one five percent per hour on average; nothing else speeds it up.

decks.domain: License loss, seat belts and impaired driving

cards.front: What is the difference between DWAI and DUI?
cards.back: DWAI, Driving While Ability Impaired, means impairment to even the slightest degree, while DUI, Driving Under the Influence, means being substantially incapable of driving safely.

cards.front: When can a driver be convicted of DUI per se?
cards.back: A driver can be convicted of DUI per se when BAC is greater than zero point zero eight percent.

cards.front: How do DWAI, DUI and DUI per se differ?
cards.back: DWAI and DUI are different charges: DWAI means impaired even slightly, DUI means substantially unable to drive safely, and DUI per se is based on BAC above zero point zero eight percent.

cards.front: Besides BAC, what can prove an impaired-driving case?
cards.back: An impaired driving conviction does not rest on BAC alone; it can be proven by driving behavior, the officer observations during the stop, and performance on Standardized Field Sobriety Tests.

cards.front: What can get your license revoked when it comes to chemical tests and BAC?
cards.back: Your license may be revoked for refusing a chemical test, for a BAC over.eight, for a BAC over.two if you are under twenty-one, or over.four if you are a CDL driver.

cards.front: How does the revocation BAC line change for young drivers and commercial drivers?
cards.back: The revocation BAC level depends on the driver: over.eight for most adults, over.two for drivers under twenty-one, and over.four for CDL drivers.

decks.domain: License loss, seat belts and impaired driving

cards.front: What penalties come with a first DWAI for a driver twenty-one or older?
cards.back: A first DWAI conviction for a driver twenty-one or older is tied to a zero point zero five percent BAC level and carries eight points, a fine of two hundred dollars to five hundred, dollars two to one hundred eighty days in jail and twenty-four to forty-eight hours of public service.

cards.front: What penalties come with a first DUI for a driver twenty-one or older?
cards.back: A first DUI for a driver twenty-one or older is tied to zero point zero eight percent BAC and brings a nine-month revocation, a fine of six hundred dollars to one thousand, dollars five to three hundred sixty-five days in jail and forty-eight to ninety-six hours of public service.

cards.front: Which first conviction is measured in points, and which brings revocation instead?
cards.back: The first DWAI is the only listed impaired-driving conviction measured in points, eight of them, while a first DUI brings a nine-month revocation instead.

cards.front: What penalties follow a second DWAI or DUI?
cards.back: A second DWAI or DUI brings a one-year revocation, a fine of six hundred dollars to one thousand five hundred, dollars ten to three hundred sixty-five days in jail and forty-eight to one hundred twenty hours of public service.

cards.front: What penalties follow a third or later DWAI or DUI?
cards.back: A third or later DWAI or DUI brings a two-year revocation, a fine of six hundred dollars to one thousand five hundred, dollars sixty to three hundred sixty-five days in jail and forty-eight to one hundred twenty hours of public service.

cards.front: How does revocation length grow with repeat impaired-driving convictions?
cards.back: Revocation length climbs with repeat convictions: nine months for a first DUI, one year for a second DWAI or DUI, and two years for a third or later.

decks.domain: License loss, seat belts and impaired driving

cards.front: When does a driver under twenty-one lose their license after a DUI or DWAI conviction?
cards.back: A driver under twenty-one convicted of DUI or DWAI faces revocation on a first conviction if they do not finish the court-ordered evaluation or program, and a second or third conviction means mandatory revocation.

cards.front: Can an under-twenty-one alcohol possession conviction cost a license even without driving?
cards.back: Anyone under twenty-one convicted of buying or possessing alcohol can have their driving privilege revoked even when no driving was involved.

cards.front: How do first and repeat impaired-driving convictions differ for drivers under twenty-one?
cards.back: For drivers under twenty-one, a first DUI or DWAI leads to revocation only if the court-ordered evaluation or program is not completed, but a second or third is always revoked.

decks.domain: License loss, seat belts and impaired driving

cards.front: Is driving impaired by marijuana or medicine treated differently from alcohol?
cards.back: Driving impaired by any drug, whether illegal drugs, marijuana, prescription or over-the-counter medicine, is illegal and carries the same penalties as alcohol-impaired driving.

cards.front: Is medical use of marijuana or another drug a defense to a DUI or DWAI charge?
cards.back: Using marijuana or another drug for medical reasons is no defense to a DUI or DWAI charge.

cards.front: Does legal or medical use of a drug excuse impaired driving?
cards.back: Legal or medical use of a drug does not excuse impaired driving; prescription, over-the-counter and medical marijuana impairment are all penalized like alcohol.

cards.front: Which common medicines can impair your driving?
cards.back: Drug impairment depends on the dose and the person; tranquilizers, pain killers and allergy or cold remedies can all impair driving.

cards.front: What should you do before driving after taking a medication?
cards.back: Read medication labels for warnings before you drive, and ask your doctor or pharmacist when a label is missing or unclear.

recaps.module: More ways to lose your license

recap_hooks.text: Unpaid child support, no proof of insurance, and an under-age alcohol conviction can each cost you your license.
The driver, front-seat riders and children under sixteen buckle up, and a teen driver's passengers all buckle too.
Delivery-van drivers are exempt only while on the job.

recaps.module: Child restraints by age and weight

recap_hooks.text: Under two and under forty pounds rides rear-facing in back; at forty pounds or more, either direction.
The twenty-pound line is ages two to four; the forty-pound line is ages four to nine with a booster.
A standard drink of beer, wine or spirits holds about the same alcohol, so switching drinks does not help.
Only time lowers BAC; coffee and showers do not.
DWAI is impairment to the slightest degree, DUI is substantial incapacity, and DUI per se is set by BAC.
Young drivers and commercial drivers face lower BAC revocation lines.
A first DWAI brings points; a first DUI brings revocation, and repeats bring longer revocations.
Under twenty-one, finish the court-ordered program after a first conviction; repeats mean mandatory revocation.
Any drug impairment, legal or not, is penalized like alcohol, so read labels before you drive.
